kcet|Chemistry|2004|18||0|0.s:
The equation shows +92.3 kJ on the **product** side, so the forward reaction is **exothermic**.
Apply Le Chatelier to each condition and ask whether it helps the yield of ammonia.
(1) Reducing the temperature — the forward reaction gives out heat, so cooling drives it
forward ✓ favourable (though too cold and the rate becomes impractically slow).
(2) Removing ammonia as it forms — reduces the product concentration, so the system makes
more to replace it ✓ favourable, and this is done industrially by liquefying the NH₃.
(4) Increasing the pressure — 4 moles of gas become 2, so raising the pressure drives the
system towards the side with fewer moles ✓ favourable, which is why 200 atm is used.
(3) **Increasing the temperature** — heat is a product, so adding it pushes the equilibrium
**backwards** and the yield falls ✗ unfavourable.
(In practice about 700 K is still used, as a compromise between yield and rate.)
∴ increasing the temperature.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|19||0|0.s:
A catalyst lowers the activation energy by offering an alternative pathway — and crucially it
lowers it by the **same amount** for the forward and the reverse reaction.
So k(forward) and k(reverse) are both multiplied by the same factor, and since
K = k(forward)/k(reverse)
that factor cancels. The equilibrium constant, and therefore the position of equilibrium, is
unchanged.
Thermodynamically: K depends only on ΔG°, and a catalyst alters neither the energy of the
reactants nor that of the products.
What a catalyst does change is the **time taken** to reach equilibrium — it gets there faster,
but to the same place.
The other three all shift the position: concentration (1) and pressure (3) by Le Chatelier, and
temperature (2) by actually changing the value of K itself.
∴ a catalyst.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|21||0|0.s:
Convert molecules to moles, then moles to normality.
moles = number of molecules / Avogadro's number
= 1.2046 × 10²⁴ / 6.023 × 10²³
= 2 mol
These 2 moles are contained in 1 dm³ (= 1 litre), so the solution is 2 **molar**.
Now convert molarity to normality:
Normality = Molarity × n-factor
HCl is **monobasic** — it donates one proton per molecule — so n = 1:
Normality = 2 × 1 = 2 N
The numbers are chosen so that 1.2046 × 10²⁴ is exactly twice Avogadro's number, which is
the quickest way to spot the answer.
Had the acid been H₂SO₄ the n-factor would be 2 and the normality 4 N — which is where
option (1) comes from.
∴ 2 N.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|22||0|0:
Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1911) is the origin of the nuclear model.
Alpha particles were fired at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were
deflected, and about one in twenty thousand bounced almost straight back — which Rutherford
called as surprising as a shell rebounding from tissue paper.
He concluded that an atom is mostly **empty space**, with all its positive charge and nearly all
its mass concentrated in a tiny, dense **nucleus**, the electrons moving around it.
The other three worked on different problems:
**Thomson** (2) proposed the earlier plum pudding model, with charge spread uniformly — the
very model Rutherford's results disproved.
**Bohr** (1) came later, adding quantised orbits to explain why the electrons do not spiral in.
**Aston** (4) built the mass spectrograph and discovered isotopes.
∴ Rutherford.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|23||0|0:
Acetylene is HC≡CH, so each carbon forms two σ bonds — one to hydrogen and one to the
other carbon — and has no lone pair. Two electron domains means **sp** hybridisation, and the
molecule is linear.
sp hybridisation uses one s and one p orbital, which leaves **two unhybridised p orbitals** on
each carbon, mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the bond axis.
The carbon–carbon triple bond is therefore made up of:
**one σ bond** from the head-on overlap of the two sp hybrid orbitals
**two π bonds** from the sideways overlap of the two pairs of leftover p orbitals
A triple bond is always 1σ + 2π; it can never be three σ bonds (1), because only one orbital
on each atom can point along the internuclear axis.
The two π clouds together form a cylinder of electron density round the C–C axis, which is why
alkynes are so readily attacked by electrophiles.
∴ one sigma bond and two pi bonds.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|26||0|0:
Three of these reagents replace the –OH of a carboxylic acid with chlorine, giving the acid
chloride RCOCl:
(1) SOCl₂ ⇒ RCOCl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑ — the preferred reagent, since both by-products are gases
(2) PCl₃ ⇒ 3RCOCl + H₃PO₃
(3) PCl₅ ⇒ RCOCl + POCl₃ + HCl
(4) **Cl₂** does not. Chlorine is not a chlorinating agent for the carboxyl group — it has no
affinity for the –OH oxygen and cannot displace it.
What chlorine does instead, in the presence of red phosphorus, is substitute at the **α-carbon**,
replacing an α-hydrogen rather than the hydroxyl:
CH₃COOH + Cl₂ --red P--> ClCH₂COOH + HCl
That is the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction, and it gives a chloro **acid**, not an acid chloride.
∴ Cl₂.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|27||0|0:
Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent, but it can only oxidise a halogen that is
itself easily oxidised — that is, the one with the lowest standard reduction potential.
E° values for X₂ + 2e⁻ ⇒ 2X⁻:
F₂ +2.87 V, Cl₂ +1.36 V, Br₂ +1.09 V, I₂ **+0.54 V**
The lower the value, the weaker the halogen as an oxidising agent and the more readily it is
itself oxidised. **Iodine** is the lowest of the four.
So iodine alone is attacked by nitric acid, being oxidised from 0 up to +5 in iodic acid:
I₂ + 10HNO₃ ⇒ 2HIO₃ + 10NO₂ + 4H₂O
Fluorine, chlorine and bromine all have higher potentials than the nitrate/NO₂ couple, so
nitric acid cannot oxidise them — indeed fluorine is a stronger oxidant than nitric acid itself.
The ability to reach a high positive oxidation state also reflects iodine's larger size and
lower electronegativity.
∴ iodine.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|28||0|0:
Ammonium nitrate forms when nitric acid is reduced all the way from +5 down to −3, and that
requires a **very dilute** acid and a fairly **reactive** metal:
4Zn + 10HNO₃(very dilute) ⇒ 4Zn(NO₃)₂ + NH₄NO₃ + 3H₂O
Magnesium, aluminium and iron are all reactive enough to drive the nitrogen that far.
**Lead** is not. It sits low in the activity series, just above hydrogen, so it is too weak a
reducing agent to take nitrogen beyond the first stage. With dilute nitric acid it gives nitric
oxide instead:
3Pb + 8HNO₃(dilute) ⇒ 3Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O
and with concentrated acid, nitrogen dioxide.
The general rule is worth holding: the more dilute the acid and the more reactive the metal,
the more deeply the nitrogen is reduced — NO₂, then NO, then N₂O, then NH₄⁺.
∴ lead.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|30||0|0:
Pure alumina is unsuitable for electrolysis on two counts: it melts at about 2323 K, which is
prohibitively hot, and molten alumina is a poor conductor.
Cryolite, Na₃AlF₆, solves both problems at once. Alumina **dissolves** in molten cryolite, so
the cell can be worked at around 1223 K instead, and the cryolite dissociates into ions that
make the melt a good **conductor of electricity**.
Option (1) states both of these effects, which is why it is the complete answer.
Option (2) is only half the story — it mentions the lower temperature but omits the
conductivity, and in any case it is the *mixture* whose melting point is low, not bauxite's own.
Option (3) is wrong: heat loss is reduced by the carbon lining and the crust of solidified
electrolyte, not by the cryolite.
Fluorspar, CaF₂, is usually added as well to lower the temperature further.
∴ to dissolve bauxite and render it a conductor of electricity.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|31||0|0.s:
An amphoteric (amphiprotic) substance can both **donate** and **accept** a proton.
(1) H₂O — donates to give OH⁻, accepts to give H₃O⁺ ✓ amphoteric
(2) NH₃ — accepts to give NH₄⁺, and can donate to give the amide ion NH₂⁻ ✓ amphoteric
(4) HCO₃⁻ — donates to give CO₃²⁻, accepts to give H₂CO₃ ✓ amphoteric, which is exactly why
the hydrogencarbonate buffer works
(3) **HNO₃** — nitric acid is a strong acid and donates its proton completely. The ion left
behind, NO₃⁻, is an exceedingly weak base and will not take a proton back under ordinary
conditions. So HNO₃ can only act as an acid ✗
The pattern is worth noticing: an amphoteric species generally has both an ionisable hydrogen
**and** a lone pair. HNO₃ loses its only ionisable hydrogen irreversibly.
∴ HNO₃ is not amphoteric.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|32||0|0.s:
The heat of neutralisation of a strong acid with a strong base is 57.3 kJ per **equivalent** of
water formed, so work in equivalents and find the limiting reagent.
meq of H₂SO₄ = 50 × 0.2 = 10
meq of KOH = 50 × 1 = 50
The acid is in deficit, so only 10 meq of water can be formed; the remaining 40 meq of KOH
is left unreacted and releases nothing.
equivalents of water = 10 meq = 0.01 eq
Heat liberated = 0.01 × 57.3 kJ = 0.573 kJ
Convert to joules, since the options mix the units:
0.573 kJ = **573 J**
Option (1), 573 kJ, is the same figure with the units left unconverted — which is exactly the
trap the question is set to catch.
∴ 573 J.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|36||0|0.s:
Rate depends on **concentration**, so squeezing the same amounts of gas into a smaller vessel
speeds the reaction up.
For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ the rate law is
rate = k[SO₂]²[O₂]
Take the same number of moles in each vessel. Halving the volume from 2 dm³ to 1 dm³
**doubles** every concentration, so for the 1 dm³ vessel:
[SO₂] is 2× and [O₂] is 2×
rate₁/rate₂ = (2)² × (2)¹ = 4 × 2 = **8**
The exponents are what matter: SO₂ is squared because it is second order, oxygen enters to
the first power.
So the reaction in the smaller vessel is eight times as fast, a ratio of 8 : 1.
Answering 4 : 1 means forgetting the oxygen term; 2 : 1 would treat the whole thing as first
order.
∴ 8 : 1.
